summary: Summarizes the impact Multipath TCP may have on applications. Although it is designed to be backward compatible, its data transport differs from regular TCP and gives applications extra options to exploit. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipath TCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. The catch is that an application that assumed one connection meant one address and one path now has a false assumption, so this RFC works out what changes for existing applications and defines a small set of calls for applications that want to know more.

questions: does mptcp work with existing applications
subtitle: What Multipath TCP changes for applications, and the small set of calls that let an application see what is really happening.

tldr.problem: Multipath TCP lets one connection use several paths, but an application that assumed one connection meant one address and one path now holds a false assumption.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the performance and compatibility effects of MPTCP for legacy applications, then defines a basic API of five socket options that let an application turn multipath on or off, choose local addresses, list the live subflows and obtain a connection identifier.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo. The legacy sockets API continues to work unchanged, and the basic API is an abstract specification that implementers may realise as socket options or as new calls.

today: RFC 6897 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It describes the API surface for Multipath TCP and points at the MPTCP protocol specification itself for the mechanisms the API relies on.

sections.title: Introduction: Three APIs and What MPTCP Changes
sections.content:
Multipath TCP adds the capability of using multiple paths to a regular TCP session. The motivations for this extension include increasing throughput, overall resource utilization and resilience to network failure, and these motivations are discussed, along with high-level design decisions, as part of the multipath TCP architecture. MPTCP offers the same reliable, in-order, byte-stream transport as TCP and is designed to be backward compatible with both applications and the network layer. It requires support inside the network stack of both endpoints.

This document first presents the effects that MPTCP may have on applications, such as performance changes compared to regular TCP. Second, it defines the interoperation of MPTCP and applications that are unaware of the multipath transport. MPTCP is designed to be usable without any application changes, but some compatibility issues have to be taken into account. Third, the memo specifies a basic Application Programming Interface for MPTCP-aware applications, an extension to the regular TCP API that allows an MPTCP-aware application the equivalent level of control and access to information of an MPTCP connection that would be possible with the standard TCP API on a regular TCP connection.

The de facto standard API for TCP/IP applications is the sockets interface. This document provides an abstract definition of MPTCP-specific extensions to that interface: operations used to get or set additional MPTCP-specific information on a socket, in order to provide an equivalent level of information and control over MPTCP as exists for an application using regular TCP. It is up to the applications, high-level programming languages or libraries to decide whether to use these optional extensions. For instance, an application may want to turn on or off the MPTCP mechanism for certain data transfers, or limit its use to certain interfaces. The abstract specification is in line with the POSIX standard as much as possible. An advanced API for MPTCP is outside the scope of the document; such an API could offer more fine-grained control over multipath transport functions and policies, and the appendix includes a brief, non-compulsory list of potential features.

Three APIs are distinguished. The Legacy API is the interface towards TCP that is currently used by applications; the document explains the effect of MPTCP for such applications, as well as the resulting issues. The Basic API is a simple extension of TCP's interface for applications that are aware of MPTCP, providing access to multipath address information and a level of control equivalent to regular TCP. The Advanced API would offer more fine-grained control over the behaviour of MPTCP; its specification is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipath TCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. The catch is that an application that assumed one connection meant one address and one path now has a false assumption, so this RFC works out what changes for existing applications and defines a small set of calls for applications that want to know more.

sections.title: Performance Effects: Throughput, Delay and Resilience
sections.content:
One of the key goals of adding multipath capability to TCP is to improve the performance of a transport connection by load distribution over separate subflows across potentially disjoint paths. It is an explicit goal of MPTCP that it provides a connection that performs at least as well as one using single-path TCP.

Throughput. The most obvious performance improvement that can be expected is an increase in throughput, since MPTCP pools more than one path where available. This will usually provide as much or greater bandwidth, even though exceptions may exist, for example due to differences in congestion control dynamics: if a new subflow is started, the short-term throughput can be smaller than the theoretical optimum. If there are shared bottlenecks between the flows, the congestion control algorithms will in most cases ensure that load is spread evenly amongst regular and multipath TCP sessions, so that no end user receives worse performance than if all were using single-path TCP. There are some known corner cases in which an upgrade to MPTCP can affect other users.

The throughput increase additionally means an MPTCP session could achieve throughput greater than the capacity of a single interface on the device. If any applications make assumptions about interfaces due to throughput, they must take this into account, although an MPTCP implementation must always respect an application's request for a particular interface. The flexibility of MPTCP to add and remove subflows as paths change availability could lead to greater variation, and more frequent change, in connection bandwidth, and applications that adapt to available bandwidth, such as video and audio streaming, may need to adjust some of their assumptions.

The transport of MPTCP signalling information results in a small overhead, so the use of MPTCP instead of a single TCP connection results in a smaller goodput. If multiple subflows share the same bottleneck, this overhead slightly reduces the capacity available for data transport. This potential reduction of throughput will be negligible in many usage scenarios, and the protocol contains optimizations so that the overhead is minimal.

Delay. The benefits regarding throughput and resilience may come at some cost regarding data delivery delay and delay jitter. If the delays on the constituent subflows differ, the jitter perceivable to an application may appear higher as the data are spread across the subflows. Although MPTCP ensures in-order delivery to the application, the data delivery could be more bursty than may be usual with single-path TCP, in particular on highly asymmetric paths. Applications with high real-time requirements might be affected, and one possible remedy is to disable MPTCP for such jitter-sensitive applications, either by using the basic API defined in this document or by other means such as system policies.

The actual delay and jitter of data transport over MPTCP depend on the scheduling and congestion control algorithms used for sending data, as well as the heuristics to establish and shut down subflows. A sender can implement strategies to minimize the delay jitter seen by applications, but that requires an accurate estimation of the path characteristics. Alternatively, MPTCP could be used in high-reliability rather than high-throughput modes of operation, such as by mirroring traffic on subflows or by only using additional subflows for hot standby. These methods of traffic scheduling would not cause delay variation in the same way, but they would need to be indicated by an advanced API, which is outside the scope of this document.

If data transport on one subflow fails, the retransmissions inside MPTCP could affect the delivery delay. Yet without MPTCP that data or the whole connection might have been lost, and other reliability mechanisms would likely have an even larger delay impact. Applications that make round-trip time estimates at the application level may also have some issues: the average delay calculated will be accurate, but whether it is useful depends on what the application requires the information for.

Resilience. Better resilience is another performance improvement. The use of multiple subflows simultaneously means that if one should fail, all traffic will move to the remaining subflows, and lost packets can be retransmitted on them. As one special case, MPTCP can be used with only one active subflow at a given point in time, and even then resilience compared to single-path TCP is improved. MPTCP also supports make-before-break and break-before-make handovers between subflows, so the connection can survive an unavailability or change of an IP address. MPTCP closes or resets the connection separately from the individual subflows. Subflow failure may be caused by issues within the network, which an application would be unaware of, or interface failure on the node. An application may in some circumstances be aware of such failure, for example by radio signal strength or an interface enabled flag, and so must not make assumptions about an MPTCP flow's stability based on that. An MPTCP implementation must never override an application's request for a given interface, so the cases where this applies are limited.
sections.plainLanguage: More paths means more bandwidth and better survival of a failure, at the cost of some signalling overhead and, if the paths have different delays, more variation in when data arrives. Real-time applications may want to turn it off, and the RFC tells them how.

sections.title: The MPTCP Stack and Address Handling for Legacy Applications
sections.content:
MPTCP is an extension of TCP, but it is designed to be backward compatible for legacy, MPTCP-unaware applications. The de facto standard API between TCP and applications is the sockets interface. The position of MPTCP in the protocol stack is: the application, then the sockets interface, then MPTCP, then one or more subflows running TCP, then IP. In general, MPTCP can affect all interfaces that make assumptions about the coupling of a TCP connection to a single IP address and TCP port pair, to one socket endpoint, to one network interface, or to a given path through the network.

That gives two classes of application: legacy applications, which are unaware of MPTCP and use the existing API towards TCP without any changes, which is the default case; and MPTCP-aware applications, which indicate support for an enhanced MPTCP interface. In regular TCP there is a one-to-one mapping of the sockets interface to a flow through a network. Since MPTCP can make use of multiple subflows, applications cannot implicitly rely on this mapping any more. A few applications require the transport to be along a single path, and can disable the use of MPTCP: examples include monitoring tools that want to measure the available bandwidth on a path, and routing protocols such as BGP that require the use of a specific link.

Certain applications store the IP addresses of TCP connections, for example by logging mechanisms. Such logging will continue to work with MPTCP, but two aspects matter. An MPTCP-unaware application uses the existing interface to the network stack and therefore tracks the IP addresses of the first subflow only; IP addresses used by follow-up subflows are ignored. An MPTCP-aware application can use the basic API to monitor the IP addresses of all subflows, which possibly implies that data structures have to be adapted and that the amount of data logged and stored per connection will increase.

An MPTCP implementation may choose to maintain an MPTCP connection even if the IP address of the original subflow is no longer allocated to a host, depending on the policy concerning the first subflow. In that case the IP address exposed to an MPTCP-unaware application can differ from the addresses actually being used by MPTCP, and it is even possible for the address to be assigned to another host during the lifetime of an MPTCP connection. This could be an issue if the IP addresses are exchanged by applications inside the application protocol, and it can be addressed by enabling fate-sharing, at the cost of resilience, because the MPTCP connection then cannot close the initial subflow.

Specifying addresses. During binding, an application can either select a specific address or bind to INADDR_ANY. On some systems other socket options, such as SO_BINDTODEVICE, can be used to bind to a specific interface. If an application uses a specific address or binds to a specific interface, MPTCP must respect this and not interfere in the application's choices; the binding implies that the application is not aware of MPTCP and will disable the use of MPTCP on this connection. An application that wishes to bind to a specific set of addresses with MPTCP must use the multipath-aware calls. If an application binds to INADDR_ANY, it is assumed that the application does not care which addresses are used locally, and in that case a local policy may allow MPTCP to automatically set up multiple subflows.

Querying addresses. Applications use getpeername() or getsockname() to retrieve the IP address of the peer or of the local socket, for various purposes including security mechanisms, geo-location and interface checks. The sockets API was designed with an assumption that a socket uses just one address, and since that address is visible to the application, the application may assume it stays the same for the lifetime of the connection. In MPTCP, however, there is a one-to-many mapping of a connection to subflows, and subflows can be added and removed while the connection continues to exist, so MPTCP cannot expose addresses by these functions that are both valid and constant during the connection's lifetime. If used by a legacy application, the MPTCP stack must always return the addresses and port numbers of the first subflow of an MPTCP connection, in all circumstances, even if that particular subflow is no longer in use.

As the addresses may not be valid any more if the first subflow is closed, the MPTCP stack may close the whole MPTCP connection, which is fate-sharing between the initial subflow and the MPTCP connection as a whole. This avoids the reuse of the pair of IP addresses and ports while an MPTCP connection is still in progress, at the cost of reducing the utility of MPTCP if the IP addresses of the first subflow are not available any more. Whether to close the whole connection by default should be controlled by a local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The old sockets API says a connection has one address, and that address stays put. With MPTCP that is no longer true, so the stack always reports the first subflow's address, even if that subflow is gone. An application that needs the real picture uses the new calls to list every subflow.

sections.title: Requirements on the Basic MPTCP API
sections.content:
Because of the importance of the sockets interface there are several fundamental design objectives for the basic interface between MPTCP and applications: consistency with existing sockets APIs must be maintained as far as possible, so that a legacy application can continue to use standard sockets interface functions when run on a system supporting MPTCP, and MPTCP-aware applications should be able to access the socket without any major changes; sockets API extensions must be minimized and independent of an implementation; and the interface should handle both IPv4 and IPv6.

The core requirements for the basic API are four. REQ1: an application should be able to request to turn on or turn off the usage of MPTCP. This means that an application should be able to explicitly request the use of MPTCP if this is possible, and should also be able to request not to enable MPTCP and to use regular TCP transport instead. This can be implicit in many cases, since MPTCP must be disabled by the use of binding to a specific address. MPTCP may also be enabled if an application uses a dedicated multipath address family such as AF_MULTIPATH. REQ2: an application should be able to restrict MPTCP to binding to a given set of addresses. REQ3: an application should be able to obtain information on the pairs of addresses used by the MPTCP subflows. REQ4: an application should be able to extract a unique identifier for the connection, per endpoint.

The first requirement is the most important one, since some applications could benefit a lot from MPTCP, but there are also cases in which it hardly makes sense. The existing sockets API provides similar mechanisms to enable or disable advanced TCP features. The second requirement corresponds to the binding of addresses with the bind() socket call, or explicit device bindings with a SO_BINDTODEVICE option. The third requirement ensures that there is an equivalent to getpeername() or getsockname() that is able to deal with more than one subflow. Finally, it should be possible for the application to retrieve a unique connection identifier, local to the endpoint on which it is running, which replaces the address and port pair as a connection identifier in single-path TCP, since that pair is no longer static in MPTCP. An application can continue to use getpeername() or getsockname() in addition to the basic MPTCP API; both functions return the corresponding addresses of the first subflow.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things an application might want: turn multipath on or off, choose which local addresses it may use, list the addresses of the live subflows, and get a handle that identifies the connection for the life of it.

sections.title: The Five Socket Options
sections.content:
The abstract basic MPTCP API consists of a set of new values associated with an MPTCP socket, which may be used for changing properties of an MPTCP connection or retrieving information. These values could be accessed by new symbols on existing calls such as setsockopt() and getsockopt(), or could be implemented as entirely new function calls; that implementation decision is out of scope for the document.

The five options are TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE, to enable or disable MPTCP; TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD, to bind MPTCP to a set of given local addresses or to add a set of new local addresses to an existing MPTCP connection; TCP_MULTIPATH_REMOVE, to remove a local address from an MPTCP connection; TCP_MULTIPATH_SUBFLOWS, to get the pairs of addresses currently used by the MPTCP subflows; and TCP_MULTIPATH_CONNID, to get the local connection identifier for this MPTCP connection. TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE can be both read and set, and its data type is a boolean. TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD and TCP_MULTIPATH_REMOVE can only be set, and take a list of addresses and ports. TCP_MULTIPATH_SUBFLOWS can only be read, and returns a list of pairs of addresses and ports. TCP_MULTIPATH_CONNID can only be read, and returns an integer. In addition to IP addresses, an application may also indicate TCP port numbers.

There are restrictions on when these operations can be used. TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE should only be set before the establishment of a TCP connection, and its value should only be read after the establishment of a connection. TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD can be applied both before connection setup and during a connection: if used before, it controls the local addresses that an MPTCP connection can use; in the latter case, it allows MPTCP to use an additional local address, if there has been a restriction before connection setup. TCP_MULTIPATH_REMOVE can be applied both before connection setup and during a connection, and in both cases it removes an address from the list of local addresses that may be used by subflows. TCP_MULTIPATH_SUBFLOWS and TCP_MULTIPATH_CONNID are read-only and can only be used after connection setup.

An application can explicitly indicate multipath capability by setting TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE to true, in which case the MPTCP implementation should try to negotiate MPTCP for that connection. Multipath transport will not necessarily be enabled, as it requires support at both end systems, no middleboxes on the path that would prevent any additional signalling, and at least one endpoint with multiple addresses. If an application enables MPTCP but binds to a specific address or interface, MPTCP must be enabled but must respect the application's choice and only use addresses explicitly provided by the application. An application can disable MPTCP by setting TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE to false, in which case MPTCP must not be used on that connection. After connection establishment, an application can read the value: false then means a lack of MPTCP support, and true means that MPTCP is supported.

Before connection establishment, TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD indicates a set of local IP addresses that MPTCP may bind to, and by extension it also controls the list of addresses that can be advertised to the peer via MPTCP signalling. An application may also indicate a TCP port number, which MPTCP must attempt to bind to; the port number may be different from the one used by existing subflows, and if no port number is provided the port number is automatically selected by the implementation, and it is recommended that it is the same across all subflows. The operation can also be used to modify the address list during the lifetime of a connection, to indicate a set of additional local addresses the connection can make use of and that can be signalled to the peer, though that signal is only a hint and an implementation may select only a subset of the addresses. TCP_MULTIPATH_REMOVE removes a local address or a set of local addresses; MPTCP must close any corresponding subflows and signal the removal of the address to the peer, and if alternative paths are available using the supplied address list but are not currently in use, the implementation should establish alternative subflows before undertaking the removal. These operations should support both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, potentially in the same call.

TCP_MULTIPATH_SUBFLOWS returns a list of pairs of tuples of IP address and TCP port number. In one pair, the first tuple refers to the local IP address and local TCP port, and the second to the remote IP address and remote TCP port used by the subflow. The list must only include established subflows, and both addresses in each pair must be either IPv4 or IPv6. TCP_MULTIPATH_CONNID returns a local connection identifier for the MPTCP connection, which should be an integer number and should be locally unique, for example the MPTCP token.
sections.plainLanguage: Five socket options do the work: a switch, two to add and remove local addresses, one to list the addresses in use, and one to identify the connection. The RFC fixes when each may be called, so that implementations behave the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Enabling MPTCP has some security implications for applications, and the protocol specification of MPTCP defines several mechanisms to protect MPTCP against those attacks. The syntax and semantics of the API for MPTCP-unaware applications does not change. However, the assumptions that non-MPTCP-aware applications may make about the data retrieved by the backward-compatible API are a concern. System administrators may wish to disable MPTCP for certain applications that signal addresses, or make security decisions such as opening firewall holes based on responses to such queries.

The basic MPTCP API for MPTCP-aware applications defines functions that provide an equivalent level of control and information as exists for regular TCP. The document does not mandate a specific implementation of the basic API, and the implementation should be designed not to affect memory management assumptions in existing code. Implementors should take into account that data structures will be more complex than for standard TCP, for example when multiple subflow addresses have to be stored, and care is needed not to add security vulnerabilities to applications.

The new functions for adding and removing local addresses from an MPTCP connection do not add security threats if the MPTCP stack verifies that the addresses provided by the application are indeed available as source addresses for subflows. However, applications should use TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD with care, as new subflows might get established to those addresses. It could also result in some form of information leakage, since MPTCP might advertise those addresses to the other connection endpoint, which could learn IP addresses of interfaces that are not visible otherwise. Use of different addresses should not be assumed to lead to use of different paths, especially for security purposes.

MPTCP-aware applications should also take care when querying and using information about the addresses used by subflows. As MPTCP can dynamically open and close subflows, a list of addresses queried once can get outdated during the lifetime of an MPTCP connection, and the list may then contain invalid entries, that is addresses that are not used any more or that might not even be assigned to that host any more. Applications that want to ensure that MPTCP only uses a certain set of addresses should explicitly bind to those addresses. One specific example is the use of TLS on top of MPTCP: when TLS compares any addresses used by MPTCP against names or addresses present in X.509 certificates, it must only compare them with the address that MPTCP used to start the initial subflow as presented to TLS, and the addresses used for subsequent subflows need not be compared against any TLS certificate information.
sections.plainLanguage: Using more than one address at once adds a few risks: a local program can ask MPTCP to use an address it should not, and the addresses get advertised to the far end. TLS is the sharpest case, because the certificate check should only be done against the address the first subflow used.
